author.name: Samuel Smiles
author.heading: About Samuel Smiles
author.metaLine: 1812–1904 · Scottish author, reformer & pioneer of self-improvement writing
author.bio: Samuel Smiles was a Scottish physician-turned-author whose 1859 book Self-Help became one of the defining works of Victorian self-improvement, selling hundreds of thousands of copies. He championed perseverance, thrift, and character, illustrating his maxims with biographies of inventors, engineers, and self-made men. His later works included Character (1871), Thrift (1875), and Duty (1880).

misattribution.intro: The full passage is authentically Smiles’s. But its closing clause circulates on its own and gets pinned on other famous names.

items.scope: “(A person) who never made a mistake never made a discovery”
items.why: The stand-alone mistake-maxim is frequently credited to Einstein online, but Quote Investigator finds no support for that and documents Smiles’s 1859 wording as far earlier (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.scope: Related “the only man who never makes a mistake…” forms
items.why: Quote Investigator records related sayings attached over time to Josh Billings, Theodore Roosevelt, and others — a whole family of mistake-maxims distinct from Smiles’s original sentence (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The complete quotation — “We learn wisdom from failure…” through “never made a discovery” — is genuinely Samuel Smiles, verbatim in Self-Help (1859), Chapter XI (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Smiles wrote Self-Help as a manual for ordinary people striving to better themselves, and this passage sits at the heart of his argument: that difficulty, effort, and even outright failure are a person’s truest teachers. Where others feared mistakes, Smiles reframed them as the raw material of discovery.

The line endures because it captures a durable truth about learning — that progress often comes by ruling out “what will not do.” It is quoted today across science, engineering, and entrepreneurship as a defence of productive failure.
